description:
## Why this is separate

Tier 3 of the from-scratch survey is not a construct but a semantics change: a value that lives in native memory between kernel calls and is mutated in place. ADR-0001 decided that state travels as binaries (HLL registers in, new registers out) and named kernel-owned resources an expansion candidate: listed in the verdict's "where defk could grow", not built. This epic says exactly how far that exploration goes before it is a decision, and which uses are already a probable no.

## The cost ADR-0001 accepted, and where it stops being acceptable

A per-call copy of the state. For a 16 KiB HLL that is noise; for a 1 MiB Bloom filter updated 10k times a second it is 10 GB/s of memcpy; for a 128 MB zstd window or a SortedSet with a million entries it is the whole runtime. The exploration measures where that line is on real sizes before any design work.

## What the one rule requires of a resource

Every kernel construct has an Elixir meaning that Elixir mode can run. A resource would need one: the candidate is a process-owned binary (the state lives in the owner process, Elixir mode keeps it in the process dictionary or an ETS table keyed by the reference, native keeps it in a resource), single-owner, with every mutation visible only through the kernel that returns the same reference. Aliasing (two references to one buffer) and sharing across processes (a data race in native, impossible in Elixir) are the two things that would break the rule.

## Exploration (do this)

1. Measure the per-call copy cost on the three catalog sizes (child 1). Exploration ends here, with a documented "value semantics is enough", if the copy is under ~10% of the kernel's own work at every realistic size in the catalog.
2. If not: the design review (child 2) decides a shape with an Elixir-mode meaning, or records a reject as an ADR.
3. If the review says explore: a throwaway prototype (child 3) on the Bloom filter: a single-owner `Defk.Buffer` holding an [i64], mutated in place, with ETS-backed Elixir mode, process-death cleanup (destructor), hot upgrade (per-library resource type, as frames already do), and the agreement property. It answers speed, safety and whether the Elixir meaning holds under tests; then an ADR accepts or rejects.

## Probably not (unless the review finds a meaning for them)

- Structures that allocate inside the kernel as they grow (trees, growing hash maps, SortedSet): they need an allocator and pointers, which have no Elixir meaning and defeat bounds checking by construction. SortedSet-style jobs stay with sorted_set_nif or :ets ordered_set.
- State shared across processes (a cache mutated by many callers): a data race natively, serialised by a process in Elixir; the meanings differ. Use a GenServer owner or :ets.
- Resources that hold references to BEAM terms (a native structure pointing at binaries or pids): outside "numbers and binaries" entirely.
- Streaming decoders with a mutable window: only through the single-owner buffer shape above, and only if the exploration is accepted; zstd/xxh3 streaming stay wrapped until then.

## Where exploration ends and "probably not" begins

Exploration covers one shape: a fixed-size, single-owner, numeric or byte buffer mutated in place by kernels that take and return the same reference. Anything that grows, is shared, or points at terms is on the other side of the line, and stays there until the review finds an Elixir meaning that survives the agreement tests.

Done when: either the copy-cost measurement closes the question with numbers, or an ADR records the accepted shape (or the rejection) after the prototype.

title: Kernel-owned state across calls: exploration first, then a decision
